amendments: 1. Include 9–16 Unit Multifamily Buildings in Residential Waste Program o Changed the threshold so that apartment and condominium buildings with 9 to 16 units are automatically included in the City’s residential garbage collection program instead of being required to negotiate private waste contracts. 2. Opt-Out Provision o Allow these buildings to opt out of the residential program if they prefer to maintain private waste contracts. o Default is automatic inclusion, with opt-out as an option. 3. Future Flexibility o Discussed and agreed to explore allowing buildings that initially opt out to opt in later, with details to be finalized between First and Second Reading. 4. Annual Application Proposal o Proposed an amendment (to be refined before Second Reading) for an annual application process for eligible buildings to participate in the residential program.

amendments: Beach Closing Flexibility • Beach will not automatically close at 6:00 p.m. • The City Manager may extend beach hours based on real-time conditions. • Additional beach access points may be opened to reduce congestion. Parking Garages and Lots in the Art Deco Cultural District • Garages and lots between 5th and 15th Street will remain open, not automatically closed. • City Manager authorized to apply High-Impact Parking Rates up to $100, starting at $40 and adjusting as needed. • Clarification added that Lincoln Road garages may also be opened under this flexibility. On-Street Parking • On-street parking on Washington Avenue will be restored. • Enforcement increased to prevent tailgating, open containers, loud music, or illegal activity. • City Manager has discretion to manage Ocean Drive and Collins Avenue similarly based on real-time conditions. Barricades • All barricades removed from Ocean Drive, Collins Avenue, and Washington Avenue. • Barricades allowed only in designated hot spots (e.g., 9th Street on Collins, and 7th Street block of Washington) at the City Manager’s discretion. Sidewalk Cafés • Sidewalk cafés will remain open by policy. • City Manager and Police Chief may temporarily close them if conditions deteriorate.

items.title: A COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE (COW) MEETING WILL BE HELD DURING THE LUNCH RECESS OF THE CITY COMMISSION MEETING ON THURSDAY, FEBRUARY 25, 2026, IN THE CITY MANAGER'S LARGE CONFERENCE ROOM, FOURTH FLOOR, CITY HALL, TO DISCUSS THE ANNUAL PERFORMANCE EVALUATION OF THE CITY MANAGER.
items.action: Discussion held. The Committee of the Whole met on February 25, 2026, to conduct the City Manager’s annual performance evaluation, which had been delayed beyond the contractual evaluation window. Commissioners generally expressed confidence in City Manager Carpenter’s knowledge, accessibility, and work ethic, while outlining organizational concerns across departments. Much of the conversation focused on the need for improved customer service, stronger staff accountability, and a cultural shift toward problem‑solving rather than rigid rule enforcement. Commissioners cited repeated examples of staff overlooking basic operational issues, such as downed cones, fallen signs, and unmet maintenance needs, emphasizing that employees should take greater ownership of field conditions. Several Commissioners also highlighted challenges within the Planning Department, noting insufficient staffing for plan review, delays in application processing, and a lack of proactive, Citywide planning initiatives. items.title: DR. STANLEY SUTNICK CITIZENS' FORUM. (8:35 A.M./1:00 P.M.)
items.action: Discussion held. 8:42:22 a.m. Morning Session • Kirza J. Raffo, identifying as a member of the Seniors Committee representing Four Freedoms Tower, appeared with neighbors from the building and explained concerns regarding information they received about reductions in donations affecting senior programs and classes. Ms. Raffo indicated an understanding that there might be funding allocated for bingo in several buildings, and noted that residents at Four Freedoms Tower play bingo every Friday and Saturday without City funds, relying instead on contributions of small items such as chips, soda, cups, and paper. Ms. Raffo emphasized that the classes offered through the senior programs were the primary concern, identifying yoga for balance and muscle strength, dance classes that include hip and bone exercises, and seated Zumba, which even a 94-year-old resident participates in. Ms. Raffo described painting as the one non-physical class, noting that it supports mental engagement. Ms. Raffo explained that the classes have grown over time and help residents physically and mentally, particularly those who are often alone in their apartments or who have distant families.

items.title: PRESENTATION BY MIAMI-DADE COUNTY COMMISSIONER RAQUEL REGALADO, DISTRICT 7, ON THE NEUROINCLUSION TOOLKIT.
items.action: Discussion held. Miami-Dade County Commissioner Raquel Regalado, District 7, addressed the Commission to present the Neuroinclusion Toolkit. She noted her previous service on the School Board and explained that she attended in her capacity as the parent of two neurodivergent adults. She thanked the Commission for raising the flag in recognition of autism acceptance and emphasized the importance of moving from awareness toward acceptance. She discussed the availability of resources for young children and highlighted the increased challenges that emerge during the transition to adolescence and adulthood. She explained that she had been working for over a decade on programming for adults as her own children transitioned into adult services. Commissioner Regalado described her family’s past participation in programs at Nova Southeastern University and noted the City’s longstanding partnership with NSU CARD. She explained that the Neuroinclusion Toolkit had been emailed to the Commission and included QR codes that provided access to the material. items.title: "TRUTH IN TRANSPARENCY" RESOLUTION A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, DIRECTING THE CITY MANAGER TO TAKE THE FOLLOWING ACTIONS: (1) ANALYZE AND PRESENT A WRITTEN PLAN TO THE CITY COMMISSION, AT ITS SEPTEMBER 10, 2026 MEETING, TO LIMIT THE LONG-TERM GROWTH OF PERSONNEL COSTS, INCLUDING AN ANALYSIS OF THE FINANCIAL IMPACT ON THE CITY'S OVERTIME COSTS THAT WOULD RESULT FROM THE ELIMINATION OR REDUCTION IN THE NUMBER OF SWORN LAW ENFORCEMENT POSITIONS AND POSITIONS IN THE FIRE DEPARTMENT WHILE MAINTAINING THE CURRENT LEVEL OF SERVICE IN PUBLIC SAFETY; (2) MODIFY THE CITY EMPLOYEE SALARY PORTAL TO PROVIDE FOR "TRUTH IN TRANSPARENCY" AS IT RELATES TO EMPLOYEE PAY AS FOLLOWS: LIMIT THE PORTAL TO ACTIVE CITY EMPLOYEES; INCLUDE A BREAKDOWN OF EMPLOYEE COMPENSATION, PARTICULARLY IN REGARD TO YEARLY GROSS PAY, BY SEPARATELY IDENTIFYING BASE SALARY, OVERTIME, AND OFF- DUTY PAY, AND THE NUMBER OF OVERTIME AND OFF-DUTY HOURS WORKED; CLARIFY THAT OFF-DUTY HOURS ARE PRIVATELY FUNDED AND NOT FUNDED BY THE CITY; REMOVE THE “LAST PAYCHECK GROSS” COLUMN TO PROTECT EMPLOYEES FROM PHISHING ATTACKS AND OTHER PREDATORY PRACTICES; AND DIRECT THE CITY ADMINISTRATION TO REMOVE INACTIVE, RESERVE, AND FORMER EMPLOYEES, ALONG WITH ANY OTHER INFORMATION THAT MAY BE DISPLAYED IN ERROR; AND (3) ISSUE A COMPETITIVE SOLICITATION, WITHIN 30 DAYS, TO CONDUCT A SALARY AND COMPENSATION STUDY.
items.action: The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by Commissioner Suarez and was not reached. Lilia Cardillo to place on the September 10, 2026 Commission Meeting agenda.

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, DIRECTING THE CITY ADMINISTRATION TO MOVE FORWARD WITH THE ORIGINAL GENERAL OBLIGATION BOND CONCEPT PRESENTED AT THE JUNE 5, 2026 MEETING OF THE FINANCE AND ECONOMIC RESILIENCY COMMITTEE, IN ORDER TO FUND UNFUNDED NEIGHBORHOOD IMPROVEMENT PROJECTS, CRITICAL WATER, SEWER, AND STORMWATER INFRASTRUCTURE NEEDS, AND RELATED RESILIENCY PROJECTS THROUGH A VOTER-APPROVED GENERAL OBLIGATION BOND; FURTHER, DIRECTING THE ADMINISTRATION TO PREPARE THE NECESSARY PROJECT LIST, FINANCIAL ANALYSIS, DEBT SERVICE PROJECTIONS, BALLOT LANGUAGE, AND IMPLEMENTING DOCUMENTS FOR CITY COMMISSION CONSIDERATION; AND FURTHER, DIRECTING THAT RESOLUTION NO. 2026-34276, WHICH ESTABLISHED A MORATORIUM ON WATER, SEWER, AND STORMWATER RATE INCREASES, REMAIN IN FULL FORCE AND EFFECT.
items.action: The City Commission considered Items R7 A, R7 B, R7 C, and R9 D together. No action was taken on the Resolution as noticed under Item R7 A. After debate and multiple motions, the Commission did not adopt the hybrid General Obligation (G.O.) Bond model (R7 B) nor the General Obligation (G.O.) Bond-only model (R7 C). Instead, the Commission approved an alternate approach: a $450 million, rate-funded Capital Improvement Plan financed through water, sewer, and stormwater rate increases, and directed the Administration to return in September with the revised project list and corresponding rate adjustments. Option 1 (R7 B - Hybrid Model) - Failed: A motion by Commissioner Bhatt, seconded by Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas, to approve the Resolution on the hybrid model (R7 B) failed, 3-4. Opposed: Mayor Meiner and Commissioners Fernandez, Magazine, and Suarez.
items.motion: She made a motion to adopt Option 1 (Item R7 B), the hybrid model.
